finding.claim: The user identity is read straight from the client-supplied `X-Session-User-Verified` header, with no session or token check in the app. Any client can impersonate any user, including a file owner, and pass the ACL checks for delete and rename. This holds unless a trusted proxy strips and re-sets the header, and nothing in the code enforces that.
finding.source: HTTP request header X-Session-User-Verified, which the attacker controls

trace.note: g.user = request.headers.get('X-Session-User-Verified') takes the identity from an unauthenticated header
ensure_allowed(g.user, f, 'delete') uses the spoofed identity
is_allowed checks the spoofed user name against resource['grants'], so a forged owner name matches
the rename path has the same flow, ending in the write at line 27

finding.guards_checked: The ACL check is applied correctly to the right object, its result is used, and there is no check-A/act-B mismatch. Missing users default to None and are denied. No signature, session lookup or proxy-stripping logic exists in this code to validate the header, so the check is only as strong as the identity it is given.

verdict.guard_found: none in code. The ACL checks at acl.py:5 and acl.py:8-10 are correctly applied (ensure_allowed aborts, is_allowed is tested). They only compare the unauthenticated header value. A fronting proxy that strips and re-sets the header could be a control, but none is visible here.
verdict.reason: views.py:11 assigns g.user straight from the client-controlled X-Session-User-Verified header, and acl.py:5 matches that string against resource grants. This gates the delete at views.py:17-18 and the rename at views.py:25-27, so an anonymous caller who knows or guesses a grantee name can pass the checks. The only mitigation would be a trusted proxy, and nothing in the code enforces one.
